cur:objects-rambona-diptych.summary: On the left leaf Christ hangs on the cross beneath an inscription naming him, with the sun and moon above and the Virgin and St John at either side; below, the she-wolf suckles Romulus and Remus. The right leaf shows the Virgin enthroned in majesty with angels and, below, three saints. The diptych juxtaposes the saving death of Christ with a symbol of Rome, in a vigorous, unclassical style.
facts: Its traditional name links it to the abbey of Rambona in the Marche (central Italy), whose foundation it is believed to commemorate; the Vatican Museums display it in the Christian Museum.
The she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus beneath the cross is a rare appearance of this Roman emblem in a Christian ivory, usually read as a sign of Rome's place in salvation history.
cur:objects-rambona-diptych.notes: The connection with the abbey's foundation rests on the ivory's inscription as reported in the literature; the full inscription text could not be verified from an accessible source.

cur:objects-pantheon-madonna-icon.summary: Although damaged and darkened, this ancient panel still shows the Virgin holding the Christ Child on her arm in the Hodegetria pose, the two faces close together and turned toward the viewer. The Child is clothed in a golden-orange garment. It has been venerated in the former pagan temple of all the gods since its consecration to the Virgin and all the martyrs.
facts: Wikipedia states that above the high altar of the Pantheon is enshrined a 7th-century Byzantine icon of the Virgin and Child, given by Emperor Phocas to Pope Boniface IV for the dedication of the building as a church on 13 May 609.
It is among the oldest Marian icons in Rome, together with the Salus Populi Romani and the Madonna della Clemenza.
cur:objects-pantheon-madonna-icon.notes: The image appears to show the panel after restoration, out of its altar frame.
